name: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme
amountText: Up to ₹20 lakh grant for proof of concept/prototype + up to ₹50 lakh as convertible debentures or debt for market entry (max ₹70 lakh per startup), paid through an approved incubator
equity: None on the grant. The ₹50 lakh part is convertible debentures or debt; the incubator may convert it to equity on agreed terms
duration: Milestone-based instalments; debt tenure up to 60 months with up to 12 months moratorium
timeToMoney: By the rules: selection within 45 days and first grant instalment within 60 days of applying; in practice often slower (incubator-dependent)
deadline: Closed for new startup applications on 31 May 2026 (final extended notice); disbursals to already-selected startups continue
sectors: Any (tech-led product, service or business model)
oneLiner: The government's main seed-money scheme: up to ₹70 lakh for a young startup, routed through an approved incubator.
what: SISFS gave ₹945 crore to 219 incubators, which in turn picked startups and paid them in milestones. Up to ₹20 lakh was a grant for proof of concept, prototype or product trials; up to ₹50 lakh more was investment (convertible debentures or debt) for market entry and scaling. The full corpus is now committed and the portal stopped taking new startup applications on 31 May 2026.
who: DPIIT-recognised startup, incorporated not more than 2 years before applying
Business idea with market fit and scope to scale, with technology in the core product, service or business model
Indian promoters hold at least 51% of the shares when applying
Has not received more than ₹10 lakh from any other central or state government scheme
notFor: Startups older than 2 years at the time of application
Startups that already took more than ₹10 lakh of government money (state seed grants count)
Startups with foreign promoters holding 49% or more
Anyone applying now: the startup application window closed on 31 May 2026
why: Non-dilutive grant of up to ₹20 lakh at the riskiest stage, when angels rarely invest
Debt at no more than the RBI repo rate, far cheaper than any bank or venture-debt loan
Being picked by a reputed incubator signals quality to later investors
Comes bundled with incubator mentoring, labs and investor connects
howItWorks: An Experts Advisory Committee (EAC) at DPIIT selected incubators and gave each up to ₹5 crore. Each incubator's Incubator Seed Management Committee (ISMC) evaluated startups, decided the amount and instrument, and released money in instalments tied to milestones. Grants are released against milestones like a working prototype; debt or convertible money funds market entry. Startups submit progress reports and utilisation certificates to the incubator.

steps.title: Shortlist up to three incubators
steps.detail: Pick incubators from the portal list that match your sector and city; the rules allowed applying to any three.

steps.title: Submit the application and pitch deck
steps.detail: Upload your business plan, budget for each milestone, and team details; the incubator checks eligibility.

steps.title: Present to the ISMC
steps.detail: Shortlisted startups pitch to the incubator's committee, which was supposed to decide within 45 days.

steps.title: Sign the agreement and hit milestones
steps.detail: On selection, sign the grant or debenture agreement; each tranche is released after you show the previous milestone and utilisation.

Shareholding pattern showing at least 51% Indian promoters
Pitch deck and business plan with milestone-wise budget
Declaration of any other government funding received (must be ≤ ₹10 lakh)
Founders' KYC (PAN, Aadhaar) and company bank details
Prototype/product proof (demo video, screenshots, test results) if available
benefits: Grant up to ₹20 lakh and investment up to ₹50 lakh
Incubation space, mentoring and lab access at the incubator
Investor and corporate connects through the incubator network
Credibility from a government-backed selection process
pros: The grant portion takes no equity
Debt priced at or below the repo rate, unsecured, with no promoter guarantee and up to 12 months moratorium
Large: up to ₹70 lakh per startup is big for a pre-seed company
Wide reach: 4,245 startups selected across states by June 2026
cons: Closed to new startup applications since 31 May 2026
Totally incubator-dependent: quality, speed and paperwork vary widely
Milestone tranches mean money arrives in pieces, not upfront
The ₹10 lakh cap on other government funding disqualifies many state-grant winners
Parliament was asked about disbursal delays caused by thin due-diligence capacity in incubators (July 2026)
goodFitIf: You were already selected and need to know how tranches and reporting work
You are under 2 years old and want to be ready if DPIIT announces a successor seed scheme
You have a prototype-stage tech product and a reputed incubator willing to back you
skipIf: You want to apply right now: the window is closed
Your company is older than 2 years
You already took more than ₹10 lakh from a state or central scheme
insiderTips: Successor schemes usually copy SISFS rules, so keep your DPIIT certificate, milestone budget and utilisation records in order
If you are a selected startup, file the interim progress update and utilisation certificate fast: the guidelines make them the trigger for your next instalment
Choose incubators with a track record of disbursing, not just selecting; ask them how many SISFS startups actually got their second tranche

performance.summary: SISFS ran from April 2021 with a ₹945 crore corpus. By 30 June 2026 the entire corpus was committed to 219 incubators, ₹650 crore had reached incubators, and incubators had selected 4,245 startups with ₹706.33 crore approved; 31 of those startups were recorded as closed. Approvals to incubators peaked in 2023 and fell sharply after, because the corpus was running out. The scheme was extended only to finish disbursing committed money.

name: DPIIT Startup Recognition and Section 80-IAC Income Tax Holiday
provider: DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry (with CBDT, Ministry of Finance, for the tax certificate)
amountText: 100% income-tax deduction on profits for any 3 consecutive years out of the first 10, for startups holding an Inter-Ministerial Board certificate. Recognition itself is free and unlocks other benefits
duration: Recognition valid up to 10 years from incorporation (20 years for deep-tech startups); tax holiday for 3 consecutive years of your choice within the first 10
timeToMoney: Recognition: usually days to a few weeks. 80-IAC: complete applications are reviewed within 120 days
deadline: Rolling. 80-IAC applies to startups incorporated before 1 April 2030
oneLiner: A free government 'startup' certificate that unlocks tax breaks, cheaper compliance and access to every Startup India scheme.
what: DPIIT recognition is an official certificate saying your company is a startup. It is the entry ticket for SISFS, CGSS, Fund of Funds-backed VCs, easier public procurement, faster patents and self-certification under labour laws. Recognised startups can also apply to an Inter-Ministerial Board (IMB) for a Section 80-IAC certificate, which lets them pay zero income tax on profits for three consecutive years.
who: Private limited company, LLP, registered partnership firm, or (from Feb 2026) a cooperative society
Within 10 years of incorporation, with turnover never above ₹200 crore in any year (deep-tech startups: 20 years and ₹300 crore)
Working on innovation, improvement of products/processes, or a scalable business model with high potential for jobs or wealth
For 80-IAC: private limited company or LLP incorporated between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030, with DPIIT recognition and an IMB certificate
notFor: Sole proprietorships
Companies formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business
80-IAC is not available to partnership firms; the 80-IAC turnover cap stayed at ₹100 crore even though the recognition cap rose to ₹200 crore (per practitioner summaries)
Loss-making startups gain little from 80-IAC until they are profitable
why: It is free and needed for almost every central startup scheme
Zero income tax on profits for three years once you turn profitable
Self-certification under labour and environment laws, and faster, cheaper patent filing
Exemption from prior-experience and turnover rules in many government tenders and on GeM
howItWorks: You apply online on the Startup India / National Single Window portal; DPIIT checks the documents and issues a recognition certificate. For the tax holiday, you file a separate application on the same portal; the Inter-Ministerial Board (DPIIT plus tax officials) judges whether your business is genuinely innovative and issues an 80-IAC certificate. You then claim the deduction in your income-tax return for the three years you choose.

steps.detail: Register as a private limited company or LLP if you want the 80-IAC tax holiday (partnerships can get recognition but not 80-IAC).

steps.title: Apply for the 80-IAC certificate
steps.detail: From your dashboard, file the tax-exemption application with financials and a clear explanation of the technology, market potential and jobs.

steps.title: Claim the deduction

Website, product demo, patents or awards (optional but helpful)

benefits: Access to SISFS, CGSS and FFS-backed funds
100% income-tax deduction for 3 consecutive years (with IMB certificate)
Fast-tracked patent examination and fee rebates
Easier public procurement and listing on GeM
Self-certification under several labour and environment laws
pros: Free and fully online
Recognition is quick and widely granted
The tax holiday window was extended to startups incorporated before 1 April 2030
Deep-tech startups now get a 20-year window and ₹300 crore turnover limit
cons: The 80-IAC certificate is much harder to get than recognition; the IMB rejects many applications
The tax benefit only matters once you make taxable profit, which many startups don't in years 1–3

Rules changed in 2026 (new definition, new Income-tax Act), so older online guides may be wrong
goodFitIf: You are any Indian startup planning to use a government scheme, tender or tax break
You expect to turn profitable within your first 10 years
You are deep-tech and need a longer runway than 10 years
skipIf: You run a proprietorship and don't plan to incorporate
Your business is a conventional trading or services firm with no innovation angle (the IMB will likely reject 80-IAC)
You are older than 10 years (20 for deep tech) or above the turnover cap
insiderTips: Get recognised early even if you don't need it yet; most schemes ask for the DPIIT number first
For 80-IAC, explain the innovation in plain language with evidence (patents, tech architecture, customer results); vague 'platform' claims get rejected
Time your three tax-holiday years for when profits are highest, not the first profitable year
Check the 2026 rules: the 80-IAC deduction moved into the Income-tax Act, 2025 from April 2026; confirm the section with your CA

performance.summary: Recognitions have grown every year: from 10,604 in calendar 2019 to 34,779 in 2023, and a record 55,200+ in FY 2025-26. As of 30 June 2026, 2,40,092 entities had been recognised. The tax holiday reaches far fewer: DPIIT said over 3,700 startups had been granted 80-IAC exemption since inception as of May 2025, a small share of recognised startups.

name: Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) and Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0
provider: DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry; implemented by SIDBI
amountText: No fixed cheque for founders: the government's ₹10,000 crore (FFS 1.0) plus a new ₹10,000 crore (FoF 2.0) goes into SEBI-registered VC funds (AIFs), which then invest in startups. FoF 2.0 micro-VCs must earmark 50% for seed/early stage, with cheques of up to ₹10 crore per startup
equity: Yes. You give equity (or equity-linked instruments) to the VC fund, on normal VC terms
duration: Normal VC holding period; FoF 2.0-backed AIFs can run up to 10–18 years depending on segment
timeToMoney: Same as any VC round: typically 2–6 months from first meeting to money, if the fund invests
deadline: Rolling. Founders pitch FFS-backed AIFs any time; FoF 2.0 is now selecting AIFs (guidelines issued April 2026)
sectors: Any; FoF 2.0 prioritises deep tech, tech-driven manufacturing, early-growth startups via smaller funds, and sector-agnostic funds
oneLiner: The government doesn't invest in you directly; it backs VC funds that must invest in Indian startups.
what: Under FFS 1.0 (2016), SIDBI committed the whole ₹10,000 crore corpus to 145 SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds, which invested over ₹25,500 crore in 1,370+ startups. In February 2026 the Cabinet approved Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 with another ₹10,000 crore, aimed at deep tech, tech-driven manufacturing, early-growth startups via smaller funds, and investment beyond the big metros. As a founder you raise from these funds like any VC round.
who: DPIIT-recognised startups (FFS-backed AIFs invest in recognised startups)
Startups that fit a supported AIF's thesis, stage and sector
For FoF 2.0 deep-tech segment: startups meeting DPIIT's 2026 'Deep Tech Startup' definition
For FoF 2.0 manufacturing segment: tech-driven startups in a government 'champion' manufacturing sector
notFor: Founders wanting non-dilutive money
Very early ideas with no team or traction (most AIFs won't invest)
Founders who expect to apply to the government directly; only AIFs apply to SIDBI
Businesses that aren't venture-scale (local services, small trading)
why: It has made more domestic VC money available, including for first-time fund managers
FoF 2.0 adds funds focused on deep tech, manufacturing and small seed-stage micro-VCs
FFS-backed funds invested in 217 startups from Tier 2/3 centres and 211 women-led/co-led startups (SIDBI)
Government-anchored funds are often more open to non-metro founders
howItWorks: SIDBI (and later a second implementing agency) commits capital to Category I and II AIFs selected through its Fund Application Portal. Each AIF must invest a multiple of the government money in startups (e.g., 1.5x for deep-tech funds, 2x for micro-VCs, 1.75x for manufacturing funds, 2.5x for sector-agnostic funds under FoF 2.0). The AIF's own investment committee picks startups; the government plays no role in individual deals.

steps.detail: FFS money must flow to DPIIT-recognised startups, so have your certificate ready.

steps.title: Find FFS / FoF 2.0-backed AIFs
steps.detail: Use SIDBI's FFS page and fund announcements to list AIFs that match your sector and stage.

steps.title: Prepare a VC-ready pitch
steps.detail: Build a deck with problem, traction, market size, unit economics, team and use of funds; prepare a data room.

steps.title: Pitch and go through diligence
steps.detail: The AIF runs its normal process: partner meetings, investment committee, legal and financial due diligence.

steps.title: Negotiate the term sheet
steps.detail: Agree valuation, board seats and investor rights; get a startup lawyer to review.

steps.title: Close the round
steps.detail: Sign the shareholder agreement, complete FEMA/ROC filings, and receive funds.

Pitch deck and financial model
Cap table and incorporation documents
Audited financials / management accounts and MIS
Customer contracts, traction metrics, IP filings

VC partners bring hiring, follow-on funding and customer networks
Segment-specific funds for deep tech and manufacturing that need patient capital
Micro-VC track under FoF 2.0 for seed rounds up to ₹10 crore
pros: Big: ₹10,000 crore new corpus on top of a fully deployed ₹10,000 crore
FoF 2.0 explicitly targets gaps (deep tech, manufacturing, small funds, non-metros)
No government paperwork for founders; it's a normal VC process
cons: You give up equity
Very selective: only 1,370+ startups were funded by FFS-backed AIFs over a decade
No direct application route; you depend on individual fund managers' choices
FoF 2.0 money reaches founders only after AIFs are selected and raise their own capital, which takes time
goodFitIf: You have early revenue or strong traction and want to raise a VC round
You are deep-tech or tech-manufacturing and need patient, long-horizon capital
You are outside the big metros and looking for funds mandated to look wider
skipIf: You want a grant or don't want to dilute
You are at idea stage with no product (look at SISFS-style grants, NIDHI-PRAYAS or TIDE instead)
Your business won't grow 10x; VCs won't fit
insiderTips: Ask funds directly whether they are FFS or FoF 2.0 backed and which segment; segment rules shape what they can invest in
Micro-VCs under FoF 2.0 must put 50% of their corpus into seed/early stage, so they are the best first target for small rounds
Deep-tech funds must back startups meeting DPIIT's 2026 deep-tech definition; get recognised in that category first

performance.summary: FFS 1.0's ₹10,000 crore was fully committed to 145 AIFs, which invested over ₹25,500 crore in 1,370+ startups (Feb 2026). By end of FY 2025-26, ₹7,000+ crore had been disbursed to 135+ AIFs, which had invested ₹26,900+ crore in 1,420+ startups. SIDBI's own page shows slightly different figures (₹11,808 crore commitments, 153 AIFs, ₹22,942 crore invested, 1,270 startups as of 31 March 2026), likely because it counts differently. New commitments slowed in 2024–2025 as the corpus ran out, which led to FoF 2.0.

name: Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups
provider: DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry; operated by NCGTC
amountText: Government guarantee on collateral-free loans of up to ₹20 crore per startup: 85% of the default amount covered for loans up to ₹10 crore, 75% above ₹10 crore
equity: None (it's debt; venture debt lenders may ask for small warrants on their own terms)
duration: Guarantee runs for the life of the loan; tenure is set by the lender
timeToMoney: Depends on the lender's credit process, typically 1–3 months; guarantee cover is issued once eligibility is confirmed
deadline: Rolling, through member banks, NBFCs and venture-debt AIFs
oneLiner: Government insurance that lets banks and venture-debt funds lend to startups without asking for property as security.
what: CGSS covers lenders against a large share of losses when they lend to DPIIT-recognised startups. That makes banks, NBFCs and venture-debt funds more willing to give working capital, term loans, venture debt or convertible debt without collateral. From May 2025 the cap per borrower doubled to ₹20 crore, cover rose to 85% for loans up to ₹10 crore, and the annual fee for 27 'champion' sectors dropped to 1%.
who: DPIIT-recognised startups
Not in default to any lender or investor, and not classified as a non-performing asset
Borrowing from a member institution (scheduled bank, NBFC, or SEBI-registered AIF) registered with NCGTC
The lender must certify you as eligible for cover
notFor: Startups without DPIIT recognition
Startups with a past default or NPA tag
Pre-revenue startups (lenders still apply normal credit checks; no repayment ability, no loan)
Founders hoping the guarantee means the loan is automatic
why: Raise debt without pledging your house or fixed deposits
Debt doesn't dilute your ownership
Venture debt can extend runway between equity rounds
Lower guarantee fee (1% p.a.) for startups in 27 champion manufacturing/service sectors
howItWorks: You apply for a loan to a member institution. It assesses you under its normal lending rules, then applies to NCGTC for guarantee cover. Under transaction-based cover, NCGTC pays 85% (loans up to ₹10 crore) or 75% (above ₹10 crore) of the defaulted amount. Under umbrella cover for venture-debt funds, losses are covered up to 5% of the pooled investment, capped at ₹20 crore per borrower. The lender pays an annual guarantee fee (2% p.a. standard, 1% for champion sectors) and usually passes it on.

steps.title: Lender obtains the CGSS cover
steps.detail: Once the lender sanctions the loan, it applies to NCGTC; cover is issued if eligibility is met.

steps.title: Draw down and repay
steps.detail: Use the funds as agreed and repay on schedule; the guarantee fee is usually built into your cost.

pros: Doubled cap (₹20 crore) and higher cover since May 2025
Usable with banks, NBFCs and venture-debt funds

Personal guarantees from founders may still be requested by some lenders

performance.summary: CGSS started operations on 1 April 2023. Calendar-year guarantees rose from ₹220.78 crore in 2023 to ₹381.08 crore in 2024, then ₹153.4 crore in January–October 2025. By financial year, guaranteed amounts doubled from ₹305 crore (130 loans) in FY 2024-25 to ₹600+ crore (135+ loans) in FY 2025-26 after the May 2025 expansion. By 31 March 2026, 410+ loans worth over ₹1,250 crore had been guaranteed: growing, but still small next to the number of recognised startups.

name: Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme
provider: Ministry of MSME; implemented by KVIC, State KVIBs and District Industries Centres
amountText: Bank loan for a new micro-enterprise with a government 'margin money' subsidy of 15–35% of project cost. Project cost up to ₹50 lakh (manufacturing) or ₹20 lakh (service); max subsidy ₹17.5 lakh. A 2nd loan of up to ₹1 crore (15–20% subsidy) for good existing units

deadline: Rolling; apply online any time (subject to yearly targets and bank sanction)
sectors: Non-farm manufacturing, services and trading activities (a negative list applies)
oneLiner: A bank loan to start a small business where the government pays 15–35% of the project cost for you.
what: PMEGP helps people set up new micro-enterprises outside farming. You take a bank loan for the project, and the government gives a 'margin money' subsidy: 25% of project cost in rural areas and 15% in urban areas for general applicants, rising to 35% rural / 25% urban for SC, ST, OBC, minorities, women, ex-servicemen, persons with disabilities, transgender applicants, and those in the North-East, hill, border and aspirational districts. Budget 2026-27 raised the allocation to ₹4,500 crore.
who: Any individual aged 18 or above
Class VIII pass needed for projects above ₹10 lakh in manufacturing or above ₹5 lakh in services
Self-help groups, registered societies, production cooperatives and charitable trusts
New projects only (except the 2nd-loan window for well-performing existing PMEGP/REGP/MUDRA units)
notFor: Existing units wanting a first-time subsidy (only new units qualify, except the 2nd loan)
Units that already got a government subsidy under another scheme
Activities on PMEGP's negative list (e.g., certain meat, liquor, tobacco-related businesses)
More than one person from the same family for the same unit
why: The subsidy can cover up to 35% of your project cost, money you never repay if the unit runs 3 years
Your own contribution can be as low as 5% (special category) or 10% (general)

Free entrepreneurship training (EDP) is part of the process
howItWorks: You apply online on the PMEGP e-portal. A district-level task force (KVIC/KVIB/DIC) interviews you and forwards your project to a bank. The bank appraises and sanctions the loan. After you complete the EDP training, the subsidy is released to the bank and kept as a 3-year term deposit in your name; if the unit is working after 3 years, it is adjusted against your loan.

name: Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises
provider: Ministry of MSME and SIDBI (CGTMSE Trust)
amountText: Collateral-free loans to micro and small enterprises up to ₹10 crore per borrower, with 75–90% of the lender's loss guaranteed (90% for women entrepreneurs)

timeToMoney: Bank-dependent; typically 2–8 weeks after a complete application
deadline: Rolling, through 270+ member banks and NBFCs
sectors: Manufacturing, services and retail/wholesale trade by micro and small enterprises (including educational institutions)

what: CGTMSE guarantees loans that banks and NBFCs give to micro and small enterprises, so the lender doesn't ask for collateral or a third-party guarantee. Engaged in manufacturing, services, retail trade, wholesale trade or education

name: Research, Development and Innovation Scheme (RDI Fund)
provider: Department of Science & Technology; fund housed in the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF)
amountText: ₹1 lakh crore over six years, routed through second-level fund managers. Companies get long-term, low-interest loans (generally up to 50% of project cost) or equity (up to 50% of a funding round) for TRL-4+ R&D projects
equity: Depends on route: loans and optionally convertible debt take no equity; the equity route takes a stake on the fund manager's terms
duration: Long-term financing; project and fund tenures set by the fund manager
timeToMoney: New scheme; first fund managers were approved in 2026, so timelines are not yet established
deadline: Rolling; apply through an empanelled second-level fund manager (e.g., TDB, BIRAC, approved AIFs)
sectors: Sunrise/strategic tech: energy transition & climate, quantum, robotics, AI (agri/health/education), biotech & healthcare, digital economy, semiconductors-adjacent, advanced materials, geospatial, gene & cell therapy and more
oneLiner: A ₹1 lakh crore government fund that lends to or invests in companies doing serious, late-stage R&D in strategic technologies.
what: Approved by the Cabinet on 1 July 2025 and launched on 3 November 2025, the RDI Fund finances private-sector R&D at Technology Readiness Level 4 and above. It does not fund companies directly: money goes to second-level fund managers (AIFs, development finance institutions, NBFCs, focused research organisations, and agencies like TDB and BIRAC), which then lend to or invest in companies and startups. It can also back a Deep-Tech Fund of Funds and support acquisition of critical technologies.
who: Private companies, including DPIIT-recognised startups, doing RDI-intensive work
Projects at TRL 4 or higher (lab-validated technology moving toward a product)
Working in the scheme's notified sunrise or strategic sectors
Able to bring matching funds (the scheme generally funds about 50%)
notFor: Idea-stage or early-prototype startups (TRL below 4)
Non-R&D businesses
Founders expecting a grant: this is loan or equity money
Projects outside the notified sectors
why: Very large, patient capital for deep-tech scale-up, which Indian VCs rarely provide
Low-interest, long-tenure loans that don't dilute ownership
Signals national-priority status for your technology
howItWorks: ANRF's RDI Fund gives capital to empanelled second-level fund managers (21 AIFs and FROs listed as empanelled, plus DFIs, NBFCs, TDB and BIRAC). Each fund manager evaluates company proposals and provides either debt (loan or optionally convertible debt, generally around 50% of project cost) or equity (around 50% of a funding round), with the rest from the company or co-investors.

performance.summary: The scheme is new: approved on 1 July 2025 with ₹1 lakh crore over six years (₹20,000 crore in FY 2025-26), launched on 3 November 2025. The first cohort of 19 second-level fund managers was announced, and the portal now lists 21 empanelled AIFs/FROs. No figures on companies funded or amounts disbursed had been published, so there is no time series yet.
